scenes.title: Swans in the Tuileries
scenes.caption: Bread broke in small hands over the pond in the Tuileries as Zhang Liying fed her favourite swans.
scenes.body: Bread broke in small hands over the pond in the Tuileries as Zhang Liying fed her favourite swans. She was born Zhang Liying in October 1906 in Zhejiang, the fourth of twelve children of the wealthy merchant Zhang Jingjiang, an antiques dealer with businesses in Paris, New York and London. At home her mother allowed the children to speak only Shanghainese, and her father carried the family with him on his trips to China so they would not forget where they came from. In Paris her haunts were the Tuileries and Parc Monceau, with its merry-go-round, and summers passed in St Enogat, a village near Dinard in Brittany. France was, in a way, her home.
scenes.voice: Decades later she still remembered feeding her favourite swans.
scenes.turn: A tutor waited with easels for father and daughter.

scenes.title: The Foreign Potato
scenes.caption: On a quiet afternoon Victor Podgorsky came to give the private lesson, and father and daughter took their places together at side-by-side easels.
scenes.body: On a quiet afternoon Victor Podgorsky came to give the private lesson, and father and daughter took their places together at side-by-side easels. Zhang Jingjiang wanted his daughter to study Chinese painting. She insisted on oils, so she could paint everything around her, down to salted ducks and potatoes. He listed the Chinese vegetables she could paint instead, wanting to know why she clung to the foreign potato. Years later she summed up the split in a radio interview: "My father expected me to study Chinese painting, but I had a different idea." Her parents paid for her art education but never fully accepted that she would be a full-time artist, fearing she could not make a living.
scenes.voice: Why, her father asked, the foreign potato?
scenes.turn: Loose Paris classrooms waited across the ocean.

quote.text: My father expected me to study Chinese painting, but I had a different idea.
quote.speaker: Georgette Chen (Radio Malaya interview transcript, 7 Sep 1953, quoted in BiblioAsia)

scenes.title: Freedom to Paint
scenes.caption: A 1923 class photograph showed her seated at the end of the front row at the Horace Mann School in New York.
scenes.body: A 1923 class photograph showed her seated at the end of the front row at the Horace Mann School in New York. She had also studied at the Lycee Jules-Ferry in Paris and the McTyeire School for Girls in Shanghai, and in 1926 formal training began with a year at the Art Students League of New York. Back in Paris she enrolled at the loosely run Academie Colarossi and Academie Biloul and roamed the city for subjects, relishing what she later called "the freedom of painting whatever you like." The loose schools suited her. In 1930 the Salon d'Automne in Paris accepted her work for the first time, and she was twenty-four and watched over by a new companion.
scenes.voice: The Salon d'Automne said yes in 1930.
scenes.turn: A widowed friend waited for an introduction.

scenes.title: He Always Posed
scenes.caption: At twenty-one she met Eugene Chen in Paris, introduced by a friend.
scenes.body: At twenty-one she met Eugene Chen in Paris, introduced by a friend. He was fifty-two, a widower with two sons and two daughters whose wife had died of cancer two years before. Thirty years separated them and her father at first disapproved, yet they grew deeply attached. They married in 1930 at the Chinese Consular Office in Paris, and she took his surname and kept it for the rest of her life. He loved art, music and French literature, sat willingly for her, and urged her to leave sewing to tailors and keep to her easel. Her diary kept small joys, haircuts she gave him and walks to hunt pineapples and avocados to paint, alongside one grumble: "Poses so badly & talks all the time."
scenes.voice: A model who talked all the time.
scenes.turn: A ship waited at Marseilles with new faces.

scenes.title: Ship from Marseilles
scenes.caption: The ship from Marseilles to Singapore carried the couple from Paris to Shanghai in 1931.
scenes.body: The ship from Marseilles to Singapore carried the couple from Paris to Shanghai in 1931. She was twenty-four that year. Aboard, they met Tunku Abdul Rahman. He kept a vivid memory of her presence, which he recalled as "beautiful and charming," and they became lifelong friends. Twenty-five years later, in June 1956, she painted him in Kuala Lumpur. The voyage marked her shift east, from student studios to a married life on the move, with new harbours, new sitters, and a friendship that followed her work for decades after the landing.
scenes.voice: She had not yet learned to drive.
scenes.turn: A shipboard friendship would last for decades.

source.label: Sara Siew, 'Georgette Chen: The Artist Speaks', BiblioAsia vol. 15 issue 2 (Jul-Sep 2019), National Library Board

scenes.title: A Second-Hand Fiat
scenes.caption: On 7 June 1935 she took her first driving lesson.
scenes.body: On 7 June 1935 she took her first driving lesson. By 29 June she had passed her test, bought a second-hand Fiat, and began driving around France to paint outdoors. In July and August she drove to Aix-en-Provence and set up her easel beside Cezanne's atelier, beside Cezanne's rocks at Chateau Noir and beside his millstone, noting each spot in her diary in French. Two years later her work hung in the Palace of Painting and Sculpture at the Paris World Fair and in Les Femmes Artistes d'Europe at the Jeu de Paume. The car had given her a new range.
scenes.voice: A small car carried her easel south.
scenes.turn: The road south would not stay open.
scenes.visual: Paper-cut Provence landscape at noon: ochre road, umbrella pines, Mont Sainte-Victoire in the distance; a small rounded 1930s Fiat parked on the verge, door open, and a woman seen from behind at a folding easel among the rocks.

scenes.title: From Hong Kong to Shanghai
scenes.caption: After 1941 she stayed beside Eugene in Hong Kong, then in Shanghai, where for years they could not get home.
scenes.body: After 1941 she stayed beside Eugene in Hong Kong, then in Shanghai, where for years they could not get home. She was thirty-four then. Fearing for her safety, Eugene insisted on taking her everywhere he went, keeping her close beside him through the long months in the city. Time passed slowly and his strength gave way. He died in Shanghai in May 1944, still far from home. She was thirty-eight and a widow. The companionship that had carried them through those closed-in years now left her alone to face what came next.
scenes.voice: He kept her beside him always.
scenes.turn: Shanghai closed in for three long years.

scenes.title: My Tahiti
scenes.caption: Rows of waterfront huts made her shout with excitement a few months after she reached Penang in 1951.
scenes.body: Rows of waterfront huts made her shout with excitement a few months after she reached Penang in 1951. She had held a solo show of some seventy-seven works in Shanghai in 1947, then left for New York to marry Ho Yung Chi, Eugene's former aide and an old friend. The couple took teaching posts at Han Chiang High School in Penang, which she called a beautiful tropical island she thought of as her Tahiti. She met the durian there and wrote home: "I have been introduced to the Durian fruit and consider that my life has been enriched by it!" The marriage soured in bitter arguments over money and her continued use of Eugene's surname, and after a long, draining process they divorced in 1953, after six years.
scenes.turn: Tahiti could not hold the marriage.

quote.text: I have been introduced to the Durian fruit and consider that my life has been enriched by it!

scenes.title: Bread Without Butter
scenes.caption: The little Hermes Baby clacked as she typed and kept a carbon of every letter.
scenes.body: The little Hermes Baby clacked as she typed and kept a carbon of every letter. In September 1953 she held her first solo exhibition in Singapore, at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, and moved to Singapore the same year. Early in 1954, from a rented house in Sennett Estate, she wrote to friends of regained liberty and a simple, useful and creative existence ahead. She taught part-time at the Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts from 1954 to 1980, one of only two women teachers in its early years. She called the life bread without butter, adding: "I don't like butter much anyway, too fattening!"
scenes.voice: Some 1,000 carbon copies would survive her.
scenes.turn: A rented house held her new liberty.

scenes.title: Chendana
scenes.caption: She built a house on Siglap Plain and kept her studio clean and orderly.
scenes.body: She built a house on Siglap Plain and kept her studio clean and orderly. She already called herself Singaporean and settled there by 1955. Malay artist friends hunted for a Malay name containing Chen, and she chose Chendana, fragrant sandalwood. She cooked for friends, oyster soup, fillet mignon and Crepes Georgette, gave cooking demonstrations for the YWCA in 1960 and 1961, and left a banana cake recipe. The Chen family of Penang, friends not relatives, posed across several holiday visits, the father only painted in later, and she thanked them: "Every minute of your stay was enjoyable for me including the tantrums"
scenes.turn: The tidy studio welcomed hungry friends.

scenes.title: Patraque
scenes.caption: A stick steadied her for months and months after one attack of rheumatoid arthritis, which had begun in her forties and had afflicted her father too.
scenes.body: A stick steadied her for months and months after one attack of rheumatoid arthritis, which had begun in her forties and had afflicted her father too. She joked to her former student Patricia Kennison that she sometimes felt quite PATRAQUE, like an old machine that ran badly. At the Nanyang Academy she remained an excellent but strict teacher, elegant and methodical, and according to Liu Kang, she taught not just technique but the ethics of making art. In 1967 she summed up her life to Eugene's cousin Dorothy Lee, promised her pictures to Singapore and Malaysia, and wrote: "I have continued to be myself seeking neither fame nor riches."
scenes.voice: She promised her pictures to this island.
scenes.turn: A stick could not stop the teaching.

quote.speaker: Georgette Chen (letter to Dorothy Lee, 17 May 1967)

scenes.title: Two Rooms of Canvases
scenes.caption: Ng Eng Teng walked up to collect the Cultural Medallion for her in 1982.
scenes.body: Ng Eng Teng walked up to collect the Cultural Medallion for her in 1982. A serious fall in 1981 had put her in hospital and she needed care for the rest of her life, so she was too ill to attend as the first woman visual artist to receive the award. In oral-history interviews with Constance Sheares she insisted an artist had to be prepared to starve, but loved the work too much to stop – in her words, "An artist, I tell you, has to be prepared to starve." She died on 15 March 1993 at Mount Alvernia Hospital from complications of rheumatoid arthritis. Afterwards her executor found fifty-three paintings stowed in two rooms of her Siglap Plain house and gave them to the Singapore Art Museum. The house sold for S$2.8 million to fund an arts scholarship.

quote.text: An artist, I tell you, has to be prepared to starve.
quote.speaker: Georgette Chen (interview with Constance Sheares, 1988-89)
